extracted.intended_audience: Stanford inventors (faculty, staff, students) involved in disclosures, patenting, licensing, startups, or consulting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and policy standards for Stanford inventors on when and how to disclose inventions, inventorship and ownership rules, patenting costs and processes, licensing strategies and negotiations, consulting/startup interactions, and equity/tax implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to disclose an invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete a confidential Invention and Technology Disclosure whenever you feel you have discovered something unique with possible commercial value; do this well before presenting the discovery through publications, poster sessions, conferences, or other communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once the invention is publicly disclosed (published or presented in some written form to non-Stanford listeners), potential patent rights are limited. Inform OTL of any imminent or prior presentation, lecture, poster, abstract, website description, research proposal, dissertation/masters thesis (a thesis is considered a publication even if embargoed), publication, or other public presentation. The U.S. has a “first inventor to file” system and OTL will not file a patent application on subject matter that has been published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why disclose to OTL
rubrics_metrics.description: Stanford faculty, staff or students should confidentially disclose an invention to OTL if they believe their research could be commercialized for public use and benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: University inventions are typically early stage and require investment to bring to market; intellectual property protection often provides the necessary incentive for a company to pursue development. The University's Inventions, Patents, and Licensing Policy requires potentially patentable inventions be disclosed on a timely basis so the University can fulfill obligations under Bayh-Dole and to sponsors. Alternatively, inventors may place inventions in the public domain if appropriate and not in violation of supporting agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to disclose (mechanics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the online, confidential disclosure form available on the Researcher Portal to disclose inventions to OTL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While logged into the Researcher Portal, under the Inventions tab you can submit disclosures, check status of inventions, including patents, licenses and marketing efforts, and update contact information (provide Stanford email and alternate personal email/phone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventorship is a matter of law, depending on what is specifically claimed in the patent as written; authorship of publications and inventorship are distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law does not recognize individuals who merely follow instructions or simply provide lab space, funding and/or equipment as inventors. Because patent claims may change during prosecution, inventorship may change as well. For the disclosure form, name any individual who has made a creative contribution to the invention. OTL may initiate a formal inventorship determination using outside patent counsel. The order inventors are listed bears no relationship to their contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Ownership depends upon the employment status of the creators at the time the IP was made, whether University resources were used, and the terms of any related agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a general rule, the University owns inventions conceived or reduced to practice in whole or in part by faculty or staff (including student employees) in the course of University responsibilities or with more than incidental use of University resources. Sponsored Research Agreements or Materials Transfer Agreements may affect ownership. When in doubt, contact OTL and consult the Research Policy Handbook section on Inventions, Patents, and Licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government rights in funded inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention was created in the process of research funded by the government, the government retains certain rights in the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This affects the University's and licensees' rights; see applicable federal Bayh-Dole and contract terms for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling non-Stanford co-inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Include non-Stanford inventors in the invention disclosure form and inform OTL of any related agreements and technology transfer contacts from the other institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent contractual obligations, patent law allows joint inventors joint rights in an invention; OTL may need to review related agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: University claims on off-campus conception
rubrics_metrics.description: University may own inventions conceived or reduced to practice off-campus if they are related to your University work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt about whether an off-campus idea is subject to University ownership, contact OTL for advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of intellectual property
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual property (intangible property) may be protected under patent, trademark and/or copyright laws, and is distinct from tangible property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See OTL's Intellectual Property Basics page for more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical patenting costs and who pays
rubrics_metrics.description: It typically costs $30,000 to $45,000 to file and prosecute a U.S. patent application (including attorney costs and USPTO fees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the technology is unlicensed, Stanford pays patent costs. These expenses may be reimbursed by the licensee if the technology is exclusively licensed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor review of draft patent applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors are relied upon to review patent applications to ensure they capture the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You should review for accurate and complete description and that all contributors are named as inventors. Respond in a timely manner so the attorney can make necessary revisions and file prior to deadlines (typically before a public disclosure).

rubrics_metrics.name: What happens if OTL does not file
rubrics_metrics.description: If OTL decides not to pursue patent protection or chooses not to actively market the invention, the inventor can sometimes pursue development while the University maintains ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases the inventor typically pays all patent costs. OTL licensing specialists can discuss alternatives based on specific circumstances; some technologies (e.g., software, biological materials) may not require patenting to be licensed successfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: What a license is
rubrics_metrics.description: A license is a contract whereby the owner of intellectual property grants permission for another party to act under all or some of the owner’s rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OTL typically transfers Stanford IP through a license agreement granting rights in defined technology to a third party for a period of years, sometimes limited by field of use or geographic region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeframe to license an invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of protecting the technology and finding a qualified licensee may take months to years, if ever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time depends on development stage, market, competing technologies, and required work/money to bring a product to market. University technologies are often too early stage for industry investment. If a company accepts OTL's standard agreement, negotiations can proceed quickly; non-financial provisions often take longer to resolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling multiple interested companies
rubrics_metrics.description: If several parties are interested, OTL will endeavor to grant non-exclusive licenses or accommodate multiple parties by dividing the field of use for exclusive licenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occasionally OTL must choose one company to enable effective development; choice based on ability of a committed company to bring the technology to market quickly. Established businesses vs startups are weighed by experience, focus, and intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical licensing strategy by technology type
rubrics_metrics.description: Different inventions require different licensing strategies: basic scientific tools are typically licensed non-exclusively, whereas inventions requiring significant investment are typically licensed exclusively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusive licenses provide incentive for licensees to commit risky capital; license terms for startups may differ from large companies. Regardless of technology or company size, Stanford license agreements usually include provisions to ensure the licensee will diligently develop the technology (see Sample Agreements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor role during license negotiations
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor’s role during negotiations is limited; OTL's licensing manager generally informs inventors when negotiating and may ask inventors to help evaluate a company’s capacity to develop licensed products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In inventor startups, inventors do not participate in actual negotiation of license agreements to avoid representing both company and university. Inventors with potential conflicts of interest must participate in a COI review per University policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consulting with a licensee
rubrics_metrics.description: OTL does not negotiate or review consulting agreements for inventors; if a licensee wants an inventor to consult, negotiations are between the inventor and the company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventors who remain at Stanford and consult must familiarize themselves with Stanford and school policies relevant to consulting, ensure arrangements are consistent with University policies (including IP ownership and employment responsibilities), and follow Faculty Consulting and Other Outside Professional Activities rules which limit consulting time and require review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest (COI) policy rationale and process
rubrics_metrics.description: COI policies limit faculty time spent consulting and outside activities to balance University duties and safeguard interests of both parties and comply with federal regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such outside professional activities are subject to annual (or transactional) review by the University; consult University Policies on Conflict of Interest and Faculty Consulting policy for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Starting a company with University technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Inform the Licensing Manager responsible for the invention so they can consider patenting, marketing, and licensing strategy when an inventor starts a company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stanford does not give preferential treatment to inventors/startups, but recognizes the inventor’s role in transferring technology and evaluating a company’s ability to develop licensed products. See OTL's For Startups section for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity as license consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Stanford may accept equity from a company as part of a license issue fee; net equity (after 15% deduction for OTL administrative costs) will be shared between Inventor(s) and the University per Stanford policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventor shares will go directly from the company to the inventors. See DoR handbook 'Equity Acquisition in Technology Licensing and Distance Learning Agreements' for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tax treatment and withholding on equity
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity may be considered miscellaneous income and subject to tax reporting and possible withholding depending on value, citizenship, and California residency status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventors may receive IRS Form 1099, CA Form 592-B, or 1042S from Stanford. Stanford may make estimated tax withholding payments on your behalf and will notify you by letter outlining obligations. Visit the IRS website for more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who to contact for questions
rubrics_metrics.description: For unanswered questions, contact OTL by email or your OTL Licensing Manager; for equity/tax questions use the supplementary Equity & Taxes FAQ or contact the Licensing Manager or company contact named in the inventor equity letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many FAQs contain links to the Research Policy Handbook and other resources; if your question was not addressed, use the Contact Us page to reach OTL.
